utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is grant nigh man and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with me is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with me is my colleague, Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. Together with me is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Seated next to me is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey, my name is John Ackerman and together we represent Mr. Esad Landzo who is excused from his appearance here this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We were continuing this morning with Mr. Niemann for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were a couple of matters that I followed up from yesterday that perhaps I might deal with first. In relation to the question asked by Mr. Greaves about the signature being put on the document, your Honours, this document is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, and I do apologise, I have no transcript coming up on my computer. I do apologise to my learned friend. I not only wish to hear what he says but see it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Someone is coming to fix it for you. I think you will continue so that we establish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The first matter, your Honour, that I wish to draw the court's attention to is that this is a document prepared in relation to the arrest and subsequent detention of Mr. Mucic, it is a custody report, so in itself it is not directly related to the search itself, but I have been instructed that the way this would be dealt with in Austria is that if the judge, in this case Judge Seda, was unhappy with the fact that the police officer had put another police officer's name on this document, the way that it is handled in Austria is that the police officer can be disciplined, and apparently for breaches of public duty one can even face a criminal sanction. So the judge does not exclude the evidence at trial, he simply deals with the officer for any breaches of the law that could follow. So I am instructed, your Honours, that any mistakes that occur like this are dealt with in this way, and I understand that the reason why that is so is because it is not looked upon as being a police search at all. It is looked upon as being the judge's search. The judge is the one that is in control, and the police are merely his agents, so if the police do not perform the task correctly he deals with them as his agents, employees, come what may, but the police are not seen in this sense as a separate entity. So the net result of that would be that the judge would be excluding his own evidence, and rather than do that the result is that he deals with the police officers by other means, and he has the capacity to do that. So, your Honours, at the end of the day, it is our submission that these documents would not be excluded on this basis at all in an Austrian court, so we have the situation where they would not be excluded there, but if your Honours were persuaded to accept the arguments of Mr. O'Sullivan, they would be excluded here, which is somewhat of an anomaly. It is an anomaly, your Honours, if the purpose and object of the exclusion so to ensure that officers comply with the law, because it would not achieve that objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I ask one question? This case never went to Austrian court. Did Dr. Seda have an opportunity to comment on this deficiency or mistake or irregularity, whatever you like to call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding of the position, your Honours, is that it was handled according to Austrian law in the same way as if it had been an Austrian investigation, under the direction of a judge. I understand, your Honours, that there are some minor offences apparently, and I must emphasise always that I am no expert in this, but I understand that there are some minor offences which the police do of their own initiative, but major matters are handled under the direction of an investigative judge. I understand that this matter was approached as if it was a major investigation at the outset, as under the control of an investigative judge. Your Honour asked me -- your Honour Judge Jan asked me yesterday -- I think you may have asked a question yesterday, whether the compliance with the provisions for witnesses and so forth was mandatory or directory. Your Honours, I am instructed that it is regarded as being directory, and it is -- if I can just read what I have been given, my instructions: "Any of these alleged mistakes concern only formalities which are established to ensure the efficient course of proceedings, for instance the presence of court witnesses. Such provisions are called in the German speaking countries "Ordnungsvorschrift", which is an old German legal term which means provision, which directs the authorities on how to proceed. The fact that these Ordnungsvorschrift might not have been followed in each case by the Austrian police authorities does not make the searches, or rather the their results illegal or invalid and does not affect the admissibility as a result of the searches at trial." We are directed to a German legal author, Mayerhofer/Rieder, in a publication called Strafprozessordnung, and I do apologise, your Honour. I can give these words to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Difficult to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Paragraph 140, Enr 5, thus even if there were mistakes, violations of the provisions on the way searches are carried out do not result in nullification of the act itself. There is a further reference, legal comment Wedrac page 218. I undertake to provide those references to the court reporters. So, your Honours, the issue of control and chain of custody is slightly different to the way we understand it in a common law setting, because it appears, and I am instructed that this is the case, that the documents, although in possession of the police after search, are not really regarded as being in police possession as such. They are regarded as being under the control and possession of the judge, so the police in fact have physical custody of them, but it is the judge and only the judge that can make determinations about them, so they are in effect -- the police are again in this capacity acting under his direction and control. Finally, your Honours, on this point, and picking up what I had said yesterday, even if there are failures to comply with the law, there has not been demonstrated, in my submission,, especially in relation to the searches, any mala fides. Having regard to the fact that even if one was to strictly apply common law principles to illegally obtained evidence, then in the exercise of discretion, it is our submission that they, even in that setting, ought properly be admitted. Your Honours, another issue that was raised by Defence counsel was the fact that there was no link between Mr. Delalic and the premises in Austria or that Judge Seda had sufficient information in order to enable him to form his reasonable suspicion that there was material on the premises. Dealing firstly with what Judge Seda had or did not have, we are not -- we do not know exactly what he was told or what he relied upon, and in my submission, your Honours, there is no evidence to suggest that he did not perform his judicial duties properly and that he did not properly act upon material that was given to him by whatever source. Your Honours are familiar with the fact that often it is the case in search warrant cases that the judge issuing the warrant receives information from a variety of sources, whether they be documents, whether they be oral testimony of the informant, or whatever. So in my submission, your Honours, one cannot just make a bold assertion in a vacuum that his Honour erred in the performance of his judicial duty unless something can positively be pointed to and there is no, in my submission, obligation on the Prosecution to prove that. One presumes the validity of a judicial act unless something emerges to suggest it is otherwise, and there is nothing in the material that we have been given access to that would lead us to that conclusion. Dealing with the question of whether or not there is a link between Mr. Delalic and the premises, I remind your Honours that in the evidence of Mr. Moerbauer, at page 3542 of the transcript at page 12, he says that at 7.00 they spotted this vehicle and there was a suspicion that this was the vehicle of Zejnil Delalic. In the course of the afternoon, at 2.15 in the afternoon, Delalic left the house through the entrance at Taubergasse 15, and he came through the exit of the club rooms, went to the vehicle with the German licence plates and drove to Koppstrasse. There he went into the premises of the INDA-Bau company, came back into the street, accompanied by a 30 year old woman approximately, with dark hair, and put files into his vehicle. So he was in the company premises for about half an hour or so, and then alone he drove towards the border, crossing at Walzberg and he left Austria at about 6.00 that afternoon. This was reportedly on March 16th . I am told line 12. Further, your Honours, it is our submission that a suggestion that there is no link between Mr. Delalic and the premises in Austria and the documents that were seized, does not sit well in the mouth of counsel for Mr. Delalic in view of the motions that they have filed. They have filed, your Honours, two motions in relation to this matter, one on 26th May 1996, and one on 5th June 1996. In the motion of 28th May 1996, in paragraph 5 of their motion they say as follows, and I shall read it out to your Honours, this is on page 3 of the English translation: "Carrying out the Prosecutor's orders, the authorities of the Federal Republic of Germany and the republic of Austria searched Zejnil Delalic's flats and business premises in Munich and Vienna. On this occasion they seized a large quantity of evidence which belonged to Mr. Delalic and to third persons entirely unconnected with the matter under investigation. More than 80 videotapes were seized, most of them the property of BH Society of Vienna, as well as the business documents, the archives of business firms co-owned or managed by Zejnil Delalic; the personal files of the employees of these firms and other documents." In the motion that they filed on 5th June 1996, they say in the sixth to last paragraph of the motion: "In accordance with Rule 73, paragraph (A) sub-paragraph (iii) of the rules of procedure and evidence, in my capacity as the Defence counsel of the accused, Mr. Zejnil Delalic, I would like to supplement my motion of 28th May 1996 with a proposal to exclude all the evidence obtained from and having belonged to the accused and to determine that it cannot be used to the disadvantage of the accused. At the arrest on 18th March 1996, the relevant authorities of the republic of Austria seized from the apartment and the office of the accused, Mr. Zejnil Delalic, a number of videotapes, documents, personal files et cetera, and similar things were also taken from his office in Munich." So in our submission, your Honours, not only on the face of the evidence is there a clear link between Mr. Delalic and these premises in Austria, not only do the documents speak for themselves in that regard, but Defence counsel for Mr. Delalic themselves do not seem to be coy about the fact that he is directly linked to these premises; otherwise what entitlement would they have to have these documents handed back? Your Honours, counsel spent a great deal of time expounding the irregularities in using Sanda Mucic as a witness because she was not an adult and in drawing the court's attention to the fact that somehow the Prosecution's case is found wanting because Unger and Winkelmann were not called to give evidence concerning the seizure of documents at the premises Taubergasse 14, Door 15, being the premises in which the Prosecution says and the Defence say materials belonging to Mr. Delalic were seized. Your Honours, this may be an interesting submission by the Defence, but in our submission, it is totally irrelevant; the reason being that the Prosecution has no intention of seeking to tender any material received or seized by the police at the premises Taubergasse 14, Door 15. So, your Honours, any talk of employing Sanda Mucic as a witness, of failing to call Unger and Winkelmann, of multiplicity of sports bags, be they one, two or other, of the 30 video cassettes, of the fact the plastic bags were used to cart the material and placed in miscellaneous boxes, the green folders could not be located as subsequent occasions all may be interesting, but in our submission is totally irrelevant. There was also a suggestion, it would seem, that the placing of the stickers on the files on 18th March 1996 was incorrectly carried out because on that night not every document or item had stickers placed on them. This took place over a period of days. Your Honours, I am sure we have all been involved in large fraud cases where thousands upon thousands of documents are seized and where the itemisation and classification of them can take, in one case in which I was involved, up to 12 months. So in my submission, your Honour, the period of time is also irrelevant, how long it takes. Yesterday, your Honour, we heard from Mr. Ackerman that your Honours should not be unduly swayed by the determinations of the Nuremberg courts, and he said this because of the length of time. No doubt there is a point in that. But, your Honours, if Mr. Ackerman had had the privilege in appearing before the Appeal Chamber of this Tribunal, he would discover that the Appeal Chamber places a great deal of weight on what is said and what had been said at Nuremberg and it is not dismissed lightly. When I suggested to you yesterday that the rules for procedure and evidence of this Tribunal and the decisions of this Tribunal come first in terms of relying upon authority, but that next down the list from that was Nuremberg, I said so because that in our submission has been basically the approach that has been adopted by the court, by the Appeal Chamber of this Tribunal in examining issues of law. Certainly that Chamber does not dismiss lightly the principles that emerged at Nuremberg. In my submission, one would need some guidance or comment from the Appeal Chamber that no longer were the Nuremberg principles to be given a great deal of weight before it would be safe to disregard them. So, your Honours, when I referred your Honours to the Krupp case, I did so having regard to the fact that on the present practice of the Court of Appeal, your Honours may well be assisted by having regard to what is said at Nuremberg, considering that is the approach that they take. In relation to the issue of captured documents, the Krupp case which I referred to part of, but dealing especially with captured documents, said the following: "The Tribunal's feeling is that this goes to a matter of weight rather than to admissibility. As long as it is conceded that this is a captured document and that gets also to the question of probative value." That is at page 648 of the judgment. Your Honours, in the Nuremberg situation, and I am speaking now more of general principle, but I think it is very helpful, in the Nuremberg situation, the allied powers captured vast quantities of documents which were relied upon by the Tribunal in its pursuit of the truth. Maybe not in this case, but certainly in cases that come before this Tribunal, the opportunity will be presented to the Tribunal to consider documents captured by one side or other to the combatants in Yugoslavia; in other words, when an army captures a particular piece of territory, they take documents that they capture in the process. Often those documents find their way here to the Tribunal. The Office of the Prosecutor or the Tribunal have no control at all over those armies and over the procedures that they adopt in securing documents or capturing documents when they win territory. In exactly the same way as the allied powers had no control over what the Nazis were doing with their documents prior to their capture in 1944 and 1945. So, your Honours, it seems illogical, in my respectful submission, to impose conditions on admissibility, especially in respect to chain evidence, in circumstances that operate in times of war and in times of conflict. The primary objective that confronts your Honours is the search for the truth and in that pursuit, ensuring that the accused receives a fair trial. Strict adherence to principles which work well, perhaps, in peaceful settings cannot readily be applied or adapted in a Tribunal that operates in the environment in which we operate. So, your Honours, if securing a fair trial, the pursuit of the truth is the principal objective, then, your Honours, that objective may be frustrated if restrictive rules of admissibility are thrown up to prevent your Honours from having access to material that may otherwise assist you. Your Honours, with respect to some of the documents that were captured at these premises, I would like to make two short points. Firstly, some of the captured documents have already been authenticated by Mr. Delalic in the record of interview, so it is not true to say that none of the documents -- not one of the documents have been authenticated. He himself has authenticated some of the documents that were captured at his premises. In relation to this whole question of the legality of the search and otherwise, your Honours dealing with exhibits 105 to 108, which documents were recovered as a consequence of the search of these premises, said, and if I can quote from the transcript at page 3927, line 6 and following. This is your Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte, addressing these exhibits at the time that were sought to be tendered through

utterances.speaker: MR. MOERBAUER
utterances.text: "The Defence also has objected on the grounds of non-compliance with the procedural laws of Austria, thereby rendering it inadmissable. We refer to the position adopted by this Trial Chamber, we are not bound by the rules of evidence. We consider evidence which is relevant and probative of the evidence accompanying it. We are satisfied that the passports and ID cards were recovered by the witness. They are therefore relevant to the trial and this witness is therefore in a position to tender them. We therefore admit them into evidence as Exhibits 105 through 108." Much has been said, your Honours, about this question of beyond reasonable doubt in terms of the admissibility of documents. The Prosecution has never shied away from its responsibility to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt and to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. What we say, however, is that this does not occur at the time of admissibility of documents. I seek to gain further support for this proposition from the decision of the Tadic Appeal Chamber in the Defence motion on hearsay of 5th August 1996, when at paragraph 18, page 8, their Honours McDonald and Vohrah said: "Moreover, sub-rule 89(D) provides further protection against prejudice to the Defence, for if evidence has been admitted as relevant and having probative value, it may later be excluded. Pursuant to this sub-rule, the trial judge has the opportunity to consider evidence, place it in the context of the trial, and then exclude it if it is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." Judge Stephen said, at page 4 of his judgment, of his separate opinion: "It is to be noted that sub-rule (D) [89(D)] while it may be applicable to some instances of hearsay evidence, is by no means confined to such evidence. It will obviously also have a role to play where, for example, highly prejudicial first hand testimony is for any of a multitude of reasons to be accorded very little weight because of the low probative value, and should therefore be excluded from the evidence." In my submission, your Honours, the judges in the Tadic decision on hearsay both speak of the admissibility of evidence, whether it be documents or testimony, and then its subsequent exclusion. In my submission, that opportunity would not be readily available at all to the judges if the evidence was proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and in my submission, that clearly demonstrates that proof beyond a reasonable doubt is not a matter that occurs at the admission stage. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt occurs, as Rule 87 says, at the time of the Tribunal's deliberation, and if your Honours wish to rely upon a document at that stage in order to determine the guilt of an accused, you must be satisfied that that document has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt before you can do so, but it does not happen, in my submission, at the admission stage and I respectfully rely upon the decision in Tadic for that purpose. Unless I can assist your Honours, that is all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there are no further questions to ask. Does the professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the contents of your own motion of 28th May, where you said these were your documents that had been seized? Do you have anything to say in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the basic arguments regarding what Mr. Niemann said will be given by my colleague O'Sullivan, but as for the questions, I would like to give responses since the submissions were filed when I was the only Defence counsel for Mr. Delalic. Regarding this particular issue, I have to say first of all that these were submissions filed with the court after Mr. Delalic had been brought to The Hague. At the time the Defence counsel was informed that many things were seized from Mr. Delalic, and that was the information that at the time we received from the Prosecutor, and with the indictment we only received statements of 22 witnesses. Using our right and the fact that we knew that the search was carried out in the apartment of Mr. Delalic in Munich and in his offices in his vehicle, and himself, for reasons of caution, our request referred to the overall space. We never talked about the apartment in Vienna or any other space in Vienna. I would like to quote this entire passage that was also quoted by Mr. Niemann. Item 5 says: "Carrying out the warrant of the Prosecutor, the relevant bodies of the Federal Republic of Germany and the republic of Austria carried out a search of the apartment and offices of Zejnil Delalic in Munich and Vienna and on that occasion, they seized a considerable number of evidence that had belonged to him in Munich." Now I am adding, since this is the entire evidence, and we are already emphasising that this is numerous evidence that has nothing to do with him, which means third parties as well, who are in no way related to the case or the subject of the indictment: "Over 80 videotapes were seized, of which most belonged to the BH Association in Vienna, business files, documents of companies that were co-owned by Delalic or where he had authorisations." This is Munich: "Personnel files for the companies and other files", so this passage is general. We learned that searches were carried out, that 1,730 documents were seized in Munich alone. At the time we did not know that, but while disclosing evidence towards the end of the year the Prosecutor gave us the entire file of over 3,000 pages. Therefore, your Honours, we do not know at all for about 40 indictments in this file whether they have anything to do with the location where Zejnil Delalic had been the owner, co-owner, or tenant, so in this multitude of documents, with all the illegalities we have found out from the statements of witnesses and the interruption of chain of custody of evidence from one location to the other, this motion does not indicate that those locations and those objects could be related to Zejnil Delalic. I just wish to say something else, a fact that my colleague would be unable to speak about. That is the fact that Mr. Niemann emphasised in the letter forwarded to the Defence counsel on 28th August, which he repeated before the Trial Chamber, claiming that some of the documents allegedly originating from the INDA-Bau company, Zejnil Delalic has already identified and confirmed them during his interview in Scheveningen on 22nd and 23rd August. In the interview, accepted by this Trial Chamber as evidence 99, there is something that is not identical to what Mr. Niemann was speaking about before this Chamber. For that reason, I expressed doubt that some of the documents in this file are not originating just from Vienna but perhaps from Munich as well, and perhaps even from Bosnia, because if we look at this evidence indicated as Exhibit 99, you will see that on that occasion, Mr. Delalic was presented with one of the documents; however, this document, presented at the time, described in detail in the interview Mr. Delalic had given, is not a document contained in this file. That is a document with identifications easy to recognise, a document that could have been found in any location or brought to that location which Mr. Delalic did identify, but the use of it could be based on its identification on the basis of the interview and not because the document was allegedly found in Vienna. I do say, and this can be confirmed easily, that the document presented during the interview with easily recognised identifications is not in this file, and if the Prosecutor claims that this document is in this file then I have to say that the identifications that were discussed during the interview were removed from the document; also one of the four documents presented at the time to Mr. Delalic, according to the Prosecutor is in this file, since there is a video recording, transcript in the Bosnian language and a transcript in the English language of this interview, we can see that when the investigator presented this document to Mr. Delalic at the time, I took a document of two pages and not one, as it is stated in the file, and I said that this was a document that I had submitted together with a submission to this court. Therefore, another of the four documents that could be used before this court because it was identified by Mr. Delalic expresses even more the doubt regarding how some of the documents came into this file. That is why I wanted to explain these facts and once again, through the evidence that my defendant confirmed as evidence he could identify, we cannot confirm the legality or illegality of the document and tendering these documents in this way to this court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise to my feet because, when quoting from the motion, Madam Residovic said, and I really have to draw this to your Honours' attention, she was reading it, and she said: "On this occasion, they seized a large quantity of evidence which belonged to Mr. Delalic", and then she inserted "at Munich". I invite her to go back and read it again, and see whether the words "at Munich" appear after the words "Mr. Delalic". I invite your Honours to look at the motion itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose the motions themselves are available, are they? We can consult them, instead of relying on what counsel said. Actually, the real issue is not what happened around the motion, but what was said in the motion. I think that is the issue: what counsel claimed in the motion, because it was quite easy to have disputed the premises on which the warrants were executed in that motion. Maybe anything following from it should not have concerned Delalic, but since counsel has actually admitted that the premises was anything concerning Delalic, and the documents and videos seized there belonged to him, I do not see any need for considerable argument on what happened -- at least this argument was brought in as a reference to admissions, so it is not what is in dispute now. Can we hear Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I could have answered, it does not say Munich, it says in front of the name "in Munich and Vienna belongs to third parties" and I believe the court will have an insight into the submission as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I have just said, those motions are records of the court, so we can go to it and see what really was said. We do not depend entirely on what counsel has said. Can we hear Professor O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to respond to some of the submissions made by my learned friend Mr. Niemann. I begin by pointing out that this Trial Chamber has ruled that beyond reasonable doubt is the standard of proof. It is untenable to say that a lesser standard of proof applies when we are talking about the admission of evidence or the determination of guilt. I do not need to remind you of your own decision of September 1st 1997, when you ruled inadmissable the statement made by Mr. Mucic to the Vienna police. Moreover, the prosecution during this hearing, or the evidence on this evidence, has acknowledged that they have been put to strict proof, as Mr. Niemann himself, when he was questioning one of his witnesses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We return to our problem yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My apologies to all concerned. Now I understand the problem Madam Residovic has when she questions witnesses in a common language. I will slow down. Aside from the issue of the burden of proof, this Chamber, your Honours, you are very mindful of Rule 95 of the rules. With your indulgence, I will read it again. Rule 95: "Evidence obtained by means contrary to internationally protected human rights. No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." To ensure that the Trial Chamber carries out its direction and duties under Rule 95, your Honours are aware of Articles 20 and 21 of the statute. This rule and these articles are designed to ensure that evidence that is admitted is reliable. I refer to the annotated publication prepared by Mr. Jones on the rules and on the statute. I read the footnote to Rule 95 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do hesitate to interrupt counsel, but there is a notation on the front of that publication which I would you invite counsel to look at, under the heading "notice".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should not be citing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. What is the purpose of the rule and what is the purpose of the Austrian code of procedure? Your Honours know that Mr. Niemann takes the position that a violation under Austrian law or an illegal search and seizure, the consequence of which may be the execution of evidence. He takes the position, my learned friend takes the position that exclusion of evidence is meant to punish or discipline the police for their illegal activities. With all due respect, in my respectful submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. (Pause). Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I was taking issue with the submission by my learned friend Mr. Niemann on the reason why illegally obtained evidence may be excluded by a court. The thrust of his submission that it is to discipline or punish the police, so they do not do it again, so they are made more aware of following procedures under their own criminal procedures. In my submission, I strongly disagree with Mr. Niemann's submissions. Rather, the reason for excluding evidence which is illegally obtained is twofold, and they are connected. The first is to ensure a fair trial for the accused. Applications under our statutes, our rules, under public international law conventions, is to ensure and protect the accused, not to punish the police in a country. Tied to that and the notion of a fair trial is that we have rules of procedure, criminal procedures in states that are meant -- are designed to ensure that evidence is trustworthy or reliable; in other words, it is to ensure, your Honours, that a court of law can rely on the trustworthiness, the authenticity, the reliability of evidence. We ask police to perform their duties; we ask them to record their duties; we ask them to follow the law when they do it, and when they do not that evidence becomes unreliable. It affects a fair trial. That is why the Prosecution is put to strict proof of showing a court, your Honours, such things that warrants are properly issued, that the Austrian law is complied with, that witnesses are present as according to their own documents, their own Niederschrift, there is a place for witnesses to sign; that under the Austrian code in particular, there is a provision for sealing items before leaving a premises. The Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the chain of custody is established; again, to ensure reliability for your Honours. Those are the reasons why courts may exclude evidence, to ensure a fair trial, the rights of the defendant, to ensure that the evidence is trustworthy and reliable. For Mr. Niemann to say yesterday that countries like Austria would ignore a decision of this Tribunal, because you have no teeth, because there would be no consequence in what you did here, there would be no punishment of police officers in Austria, is not only an insult to this Tribunal but it is also saying that this Tribunal should give its stamp of approval to something which Mr. Niemann is on the point of agreeing that the procedures were illegal; that police officers went out of their way to choose a 16 year old girl, that there is a mala fides, there is admittedly a forged document, meant to mislead. There is so much contradictory evidence that the Prosecution is now saying, "We abandon apartment 14". We have two bags, not one bag, cassettes change; "We abandon apartment 14". What about all the co-mingling of the evidence back at police headquarters on 18th March? That is the chain that I was discussing with you yesterday. That is why I tried to break it down into time periods. There are considerable problems with the period where the seizure begins at 14 and takes us back to police headquarters. There are considerable problems when we go from INDA-Bau to police headquarters, and then in police headquarters we have all the co-mingling of evidence, documents moving, nothing marked, not one document is marked or identified before 8.00 pm on 18th March. That is the evidence. So now they are abandoning a set of documents and tapes from apartment 14, because there the violations are flagrant, are they not? What about the events of the evening of the 18th? We have conflicting evidence that according to the OTP investigator D'Hooge, Dr. Seda, this investigating magistrate, who is in charge, could not be contacted to give his approval. He was not on the premises. You remember my friend's argument, he was the man in control. The OTP investigators were told he was not available, it was after working hours. Yet Moerbauer says, I gave out documents on his approval. The co-mingling of evidence from 14 and INDA-Bau on the night of the 18th. With all due respect to my friend Mr. Niemann, he is incorrect when he says that in regard to when items were marked -- I will just find the notes I took when he was speaking. Regarding the point at which stickers were put on the files, the evidence of Mr. Panzer is that he put stickers on all the files from INDA-Bau on 19th March, the exterior. We have made a distinction in this courtroom between the file folders and their contents. Panzer's evidence is that he put stickers on them on 19th March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You appear to be repeating your submissions yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I am responding to Mr. Niemann's submissions this morning. He was incorrect when he said that, your Honour. If you just bear with me, I think it is important. The interior of those folders from INDA-Bau, the file folders themselves, and this is the whole key to chain of evidence, according to Moerbauer, the documents are marked on 22nd April during a ten day period. He comes to this courtroom and he cannot identify his mark on all but one document. That is conclusive proof, your Honours. There is no explanation as to what happened to those documents. He was not able to tell your Honours that the documents he was shown are the documents that he marked. His marks have disappeared. By no stretch has the Prosecution proven that those documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you know the content of those folders?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, I do not. Mr. Moerbauer does not either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then what are we trying to admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is trying to say that what is being admitted are those documents. There is no proof of the provenance of those documents. There is no proof that the documents in these binders are the ones that Moerbauer marked because his marks are no longer on those documents. Those may not even be the documents that he saw. That is the obvious conclusion. My friend also talked about chain of custody in time of war. We were in Vienna Austria, your Honours, in March 1996. We were in a western country that is not at war. I think that goes without saying, with an elite police force who sent experienced police officers to handle things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They all disclaim they belong to an elite portion of Vienna's police.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: They were in charge of state security and things like that, so in fact they may not have been an elite branch of the Austrian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In pursuit of this chain of custody argument, who do you think is in possession at any one time? The Vienna police, or the commander who took charge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With all due respect to your request, I think that is a question for the Prosecution to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you are challenging the chain of -- at least you have to establish where the possession lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is precisely the point. There is no proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the provenance of these items, because of the way they are handled, coming to police headquarters. There is no proof of who handled, took or moved articles around on the evening of the 18th and when Moerbauer is the first person, beginning on March 22nd, who says "I opened folders and I put marks on the documents, my mark was on those documents", he comes to this court in June 1997, he is asked by yourself, Judge Karibi-Whyte, "Are your marks on these documents?" He says no. He cannot say whether those are his documents, the ones he looked at a year and a half earlier or not. There is no proof. He does not understand the language, and it would not be fair to ask a man, a year and a half later, "Could you look through these and tell me whether these are the exact documents you looked at at the end of March 1996?" That is what the chain of custody is all about, proving continuity, and Mr. Moerbauer's evidence is fatal on that. He says he looked at INDA-Bau documents, he put his sticker. He comes here, there are no stickers on the documents. So what happened to them, who knows? There is no way of knowing, your Honour. That is the fatal flaw that determines this issue, in our submission. We cannot know. Moerbauer came here and said, "I do not know", in response to your question. You spotted the issue, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually perhaps I might have been misunderstood now from the question I posed to you. What I am trying to find out is strictly jurisprudential, where does the custody lie in respect of all those things recovered on search? Is it on the individual policemen or in the team which actually went for the search?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We talk about the chain of custody, we talk about all police officers who had handling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All of them as a group or individually in respect of what they --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Individually, your Honour. Each police officer has custody and control at a certain point and he passes it on to a colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what I am trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is the fatal aspect of this whole issue on having proved these documents having regard to their authenticity and reliability. It has not been done and it cannot be done because Officer Moerbauer, the central man in this, the only man who marked things individually, came here and said "I do not see my mark", which suggests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I return again to whatever is asked, what were being tendered were folders containing documents. I do not know if any document was being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I would agree with you on that, your Honour. That there is no way of proving the documents. The documents have not been proven and not been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is excluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My understanding is Mr. Niemann wants the contents tendered and I am saying he cannot prove the contents. If he only wants the folders, the 12 coloured folders with no contents, I would not oppose that as strenuously, but even those are not proven. So the submissions are that there is mala fides, there is no proof of the contents of these folders at all, I assume that is what my friend wants to admit. On that basis, on the basis of all these witnesses individually who handled these items and who marked them and Moerbauer in particular could not identify a single document from those folders and those are the exhibits in fact between 104 and 147 which are Prosecution exhibits, which they are attempting to tender and that is why I raised the point that Moerbauer, the man who says he marked them, analysed them in that chair said he could not identify them because his marking was no longer there. Are there any further questions from your Honours? Can I be of any further assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue with your submission. If that is all you have, I think that is all for the argument of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours, I would like to reply to what my learned colleague said yesterday and stressed today again in his response as regards the manner of gathering evidence, and the entirety of the matter. I will not be overlong, so if you will allow me, it does affect my client, so please allow me to present my argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a little unfair. I think that this is the motion that was put on by counsel for Mr. Delalic and counsel has had an exhaustive opportunity to address on both sides. In relation to that, are we to be confronted with a whole range of different arguments that will be put forward? We have no idea -- there has been no motion filed by this counsel in relation to the matter. I submit, your Honours, it is a little unfair to allow all counsel to pop up at will and say whatever they think might be useful about these things. It is the motion of Mr. Delalic that your Honours are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually this is not a general issue in which perhaps most counsel might be helpful in making contributions. It is a specific motion under the name of Delalic. I do not think you need to assist, except perhaps if the court wants assistance. But I do not think it is necessary. We have had exhaustive arguments since yesterday. Have I made myself understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I will respect your decision. This was my request, but if it is your position that the rest of the Defence should not join in, but since I thought that there was a number of questions of principle, but anyway, I do respect your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is the end of the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will rise now and come back at 12.00. Perhaps we would want to have a short status conference at that time, to organise the affairs. As you know, we will soon be having a break from the 15th and we are not likely to resume for some time. We want to know exactly how things are organised for possibly the last lap of the Prosecution case presentation, so we will know how everybody stands, how the Defence also. We will organise the affairs following how you schedule your arrangements. We will rise now. Possibly the accused -- it is not necessary the accused be present because in a status conference, it might be helpful to counsel, but normally I do not think they need be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think there is any problem with regard to that. I do not foresee any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not see a problem. Of course, my client is not here in any case. I do not foresee a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, if possible, my client has requested to attend the status conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be back at that time. (11.20 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are giving a very short ruling on the last of the arguments, because of the nature of the decision we are handing down. The Trial Chamber has considered the contentions of counsel for Delalic and for the Prosecution, with respect to the admissibility of evidence consisting of documents and video cassettes recovered during the search of premises designated as occupied by Delalic in those proceedings. We have considered the contention that the warrant relied upon for the search of the premises is illegal. The Trial Chamber has no evidence of the breach of any condition predicating its issue. We rely on the principle of omnia presumatorite esse acta to hold the warrant valid. The effect of non-compliance with the procedure requirements of such we do not consider the situation so reprehensible as to render the acts illegal. We therefore consider it in the interests of the trial to admit the materials recovered during the search --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could his Honour please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We therefore consider it in the interests of the trial to admit the materials recovered during the search and tendered in evidence. We however observe that the Defence is entitled to address the Trial Chamber on those materials, and will be entitled to challenge the admissibility of any documents sought to be tendered as arising from the search or discrepancies from evidence of witnesses. This is because the Prosecution is seeking to tender 12 folders containing documents, but not the documents contained therein. To adopt another approach would be tantamount to reviewing a considerable portion of the case, an exercise clearly undesirable in the overall determination of the case, which should not be decided piecemeal. The Defence is entitled to challenge any of the evidence when tendered. They still reserve the right to challenge any other issues which are not involved in this decision. I think this is our decision. We will carry on in this way. We will deliver our ruling on the Mucic admissibility letter later on, not now. We can now go into the status conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, to make sure that it is clear to me in this phase, this was your decision regarding the documents and 12 folders. However, in the proposal of the Prosecution -- in the motion of the Prosecution, there were three videotapes that Mr. Navrat, the only witness from the location, could neither identify nor recognise, nor did the Prosecutor propose that to the witness, and in your decision I did not hear whether you decided -- whether you have already ruled on the three videotapes whose number changed from the time of the seizure to the time they departed from the police station, so I would like to ask you if I misunderstood, because I thought the ruling referred only to the documents. I would like to have a clarification at this point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I said was consisting of documents and video cassettes. That was what I said. Perhaps the transcript will show that. (In closed session) Pages 7409 to 7417 in closed session (12.30 pm) (Court adjourned until 10.00 am on Monday, 6th October 1997)
